final_answer:
Short answer: probably no on both. On these facts Client most likely cannot stop paying, and Lessor is most likely not responsible for the defective Trailers. Client's remedy lies against Manufacturer, and that is now largely a bankruptcy claim.

1. The Lease is probably a 'finance lease' under Virginia's UCC Article 2A (Va. Code 8.2A-103(1)(g)). The definition has three parts: the lessor does not select, manufacture or supply the goods; the lessor acquires the goods in connection with the lease; and one of several conditions is met. Here Client, not Lessor, picked the model and negotiated the refrigeration specs. Lessor only bought the Trailers from Manufacturer and leased them. Lessor also gave Client a complete copy of the supply contract, including the warranty, before Client signed. That satisfies the uniform text's alternative condition of delivering the supply contract before signing. I could not retrieve the full Virginia text, so the third prong rests on the uniform text and a search summary of the Virginia section. Please confirm it against the statute. A lease for business use, as here, is not a consumer lease.

2. Hell-or-high-water. Under 8.2A-407, in a finance lease that is not a consumer lease, the lessee's promises become irrevocable and independent once the lessee accepts the goods. They are enforceable by and against assignees and cannot be cancelled or terminated without the consent of the party to whom the promise runs. The rule is self-executing. The Lease's 'absolute and unconditional, irrespective of any defense or setoff' language reinforces it, and the statute would likely apply even without that clause. Compressor failures four months after delivery, with no showing that Client rejected the Trailers or revoked acceptance, do not by themselves excuse payment. Client's setoff, recoupment and warranty-breach theories against Lessor are therefore likely barred.

3. Lessor's responsibility. The Lease contains no warranties from Lessor and points Client to Manufacturer. Under 8.2A-209, the benefit of the supplier's promises and warranties extends to Client as lessee, to the extent of its leasehold interest. That benefit is subject to the terms of the supply contract and all defenses and claims arising from it. It does not impose any duty or liability on the lessee. The warranty therefore runs from Manufacturer, not Lessor. In a finance lease, the lessor's implied warranties of merchantability and fitness do not arise. I did not verify the Article 2A sections on this point (8.2A-212, 8.2A-213, 8.2A-103(1)(g)). Treat that conclusion as reasoned from the Article 2A scheme and not source-grounded.

4. Exceptions and limits. These could change the outcome, so Client should check each of them. (a) Revocation of acceptance, 8.2A-517. In a finance lease the lessee may revoke acceptance only if the nonconformity substantially impairs value and acceptance was reasonably induced by the lessor's assurances. The 'difficulty of discovery' and 'assumed cure' grounds are unavailable except in non-finance leases. If Lessor gave assurances about the Trailers' condition or the warranty, revocation against Lessor may be possible. Nothing in the facts suggests that. (b) Good faith, 8.2A-103(4), applies to enforcement. (c) Unconscionability and fraud remain available in principle. (d) If the lease is not a finance lease, for example because Lessor in fact helped select the goods or the three-part definition is not met, 8.2A-407 does not apply. The Lease's own hell-or-high-water clause is then a contract term. Lessor may then face implied warranty exposure subject to any disclaimer, and the independence of Client's payment duty becomes contestable. (e) The Lease's own wording. This answer assumes the clause is as quoted and that there is no conflicting term, such as a remedy for Lessor's own acts.

5. Consequences of stopping payment. Non-payment is a default under the Lease. Under the Article 2A default scheme (8.2A-523 and following), Lessor may accelerate, repossess, and recover damages. Lessor's claim could be roughly 60 months of rent at $2,200 per trailer (about $264,000 per trailer over the term, discounted and net of resale credit) plus costs. The Lease's own default and fee terms control. I did not research those sections, so Client should read the Lease's remedies and fee clauses.

6. Client's real recourse. Client holds warranty claims against Manufacturer. Because Manufacturer is in Chapter 7 and the trustee will not honor warranty claims, Client's claim is a general unsecured claim in the bankruptcy. A proof of claim should be filed by the claims bar date. Client should also pursue alternatives: any component-manufacturer warranties, any extended-warranty or insurer coverage, repairs at its own cost, and, if applicable, any statutory or equitable remedy against third parties. Lessor's practical position, as financier, is not worse for the supplier's insolvency.

7. Recommendation. Client should resume payments, or at a minimum negotiate with Lessor. It should reserve its rights, file the proof of claim, and gather evidence of Lessor's assurances, if any. It should have counsel read the Lease and the full Virginia text of the cited sections. Caveat: my source verification was limited. Virginia-site and Cornell fetches were blocked, so the statutory propositions rest on search-result text of the Virginia and uniform provisions, not on full-page review. I found no Virginia appellate case applying 8.2A-407.

authorities.title: Irrevocable promises: finance leases
authorities.proposition: In a non-consumer finance lease, lessee's promises become irrevocable and independent on acceptance and are enforceable, not subject to cancellation or termination without consent.

authorities.proposition: In a finance lease, revocation of acceptance is available on lessor's assurances but not on difficulty of discovery or assumed cure.

claims.text: The Lease is likely a finance lease under 8.2A-103(1)(g), since Client selected and negotiated and Lessor only financed and gave the supply contract before signing.
Under 8.2A-407, Client's rent obligation became irrevocable and independent on acceptance, so the compressor failures do not suspend payment against Lessor.
Lessor gave no warranties; Client's warranty rights run against Manufacturer through 8.2A-209, so Lessor is likely not responsible for the defects.
Narrow exceptions exist, chiefly revocation of acceptance based on Lessor's assurances, good faith, and non-finance-lease status, and none is indicated by the facts.
Stopping payment is a default exposing Client to Lessor remedies; Client's remedy is an unsecured claim in Manufacturer's Chapter 7.
